new_statements.rule_in_words: Ngundu, like all Banda varieties in the 1978 survey, is described as a tone language with three level registers and open (CV) syllables; the source (a wordlist-based segmental sketch) says nothing about word stress or accent — full-text probes find no occurrence of accent/tonique/intonation/prosodique/intensité anywhere in the volume. No source states a stress locus for Ngundu; the nearest Banda statements are generic (Tucker & Bryan 1966: Banda penultimate tends to 'extra shortness') or about other Banda languages (Cotel 1907 Togbo: accent mostly penultimate; Sampson 1985 Tangbago: stress non-contrastive, governed by tone and word shape).
new_statements.domain_note: Tone statement is a group-level generalisation over eleven Banda varieties from 79-175-item wordlists (citation forms); Ngundu data = 175-item QIL list from Bianga (Basse-Kotto, CAR). Seen only as scanned search snippets, not full pages.
new_statements.identity_note: Glottolog's one 'descriptive' ref for ngun1266 (Faust & Grossman 2023 'Nuer') is a mis-link (Nuer = nus) and irrelevant. The only first-hand Ngundu material is Cloarec-Heiss 1978's 'ngündù (de Bianga)' — Bianga, Basse-Kotto, Central African Republic, which matches Glottolog's coordinates (4.89N 20.42E); Ethnologue instead lists Ngundu [nue] as a DR Congo language (5,100), which Olson 2001:5 says has 'no present-day evidence'. All accessible prosodic statements are about other Banda languages: Mono [mnh] = mono1270 (Olson 2001, 2004; Kamanda-Kola 2003), Togbo (Cotel 1907) = togb1241, Banda-Tangbago (Sampson 1985) under band1342, generic 'BANDA' (Tucker & Bryan 1966). Ethnologue's 'most similar' variety is Kpagua [kuw] = kpag1238 (Glottolog subgroup Ngundu-Kpagua ngun1281).

new_statements.quote: ACCENT. La langue banda est chantée, c'est-à-dire, que chaque syllabe a sa tonalité propre, et est prononcée sur un ton plus élevé ou plus bas que la voisine. On distingue trois tons principaux : le ton haut, dans nó, di, ká, tout, le ton moyen, dans enji, ils, le ton bas, dans mbwängą, palabre. [...] En dehors de l'accent de hauteur, il existe en banda un accent d'inten-[p. 24]sité qui affecte certaines syllabes des mots, en sorte que les syllabes non accentuées s'abrègent et ont une tendance à disparaître : Bëleda, tronc d'arbre, bleda ; temö, marque du futur, tem ; marë, faire, mar. [diacritics on the three example words approximate]
new_statements.translation: ACCENT. The Banda language is 'sung', i.e. each syllable has its own pitch and is pronounced on a higher or lower tone than its neighbour. Three main tones are distinguished: high (nó, di, ká 'all'), mid (enji 'they'), low (mbwängą 'palaver'). [...] Besides this pitch accent, Banda has an intensity accent which falls on certain syllables of words, so that the unaccented syllables shorten and tend to disappear: bëleda 'tree trunk' > bleda; temö (future marker) > tem; marë 'to do' > mar.
new_statements.citation: Tisserant, Charles. 1930. Essai sur la grammaire banda (Travaux et Mémoires de l'Institut d'Ethnologie 13). Paris: Institut d'Ethnologie. 185 pp.
new_statements.locator: Introduction, ch. 'Phonétique', section 'ACCENT', book pp. 23-24 (= calameo/PDF pages 25-26; text file lines 2450-2618); verified against the page images. Footnote 3 p. 23: 'Cette différence de tonalité des syllabes fait de la langue banda une langue chantée. Elle peut donc être parlée à distance sur des instruments donnant les trois tons principaux.. cornes, fifres, et surtout le tamtam.' Also p. 19 ('Sons fondamentaux'): 'œ, « eu » dans « peu », fréquent en banda, surtout dans des syllabes peu accentuées.'

new_statements.relation_note: Catalog record (Cloarec-Heiss 1978): Ngundu tonal, three registers, no stress statement. Tisserant 1930 agrees on the three-tone system ('trois tons principaux: haut, moyen, bas', every syllable toned) and ADDS that Banda also has an 'accent d'intensité' on certain syllables with reduction/loss of unstressed syllables, placement unspecified. Caveat on scope: the statement is made for 'la langue banda' in general; Tisserant's dialect table (pp. 4-5) does not name Ngundu; of the Mid-Southern cluster to which Ngundu belongs he lists Mono, Togbo and Ngobu (Gobu) and cites Mono/Togbo/Yakpa forms throughout, so for Ngundu this is Banda-general evidence, not a Ngundu-specific statement.
new_statements.rule_in_words: Banda (Tisserant's pan-dialectal description, based chiefly on Linda / Banda-Banda of the Bambari-Ippy area with notes on Togbo, Mono, Yakpa, Langbasi, Dakpa) is a tone language: every syllable carries one of three level tones (high, mid, low), and grammatical function can raise a vowel's tone. In addition there is a dynamic (intensity) accent on 'certain syllables' of the word; its position is NOT stated. Unstressed syllables shorten and tend to be lost (examples show loss of a first-syllable vowel, bëleda > bleda, and of final vowels, temö > tem, marë > mar), and the vowel œ occurs mostly in weakly stressed syllables (p. 19). No placement rule, no statement that stress is contrastive.
new_statements.exceptions: none; the accent is said to affect 'certaines syllabes' without a rule. Loanwords 'reçoivent leurs accents tout comme les mots banda authentiques' (p. 24, said of the tonal accents used in drum language).
new_statements.identity_note: Tisserant's grammar covers 'la langue banda' as a whole from fieldwork in Ubangi-Shari (Bambari, Ippy, Ouaka-Kotto region), citing forms mainly from Linda and Banda-Banda and, for the southern group, Yakpwa, Mono, Togbo, Langbasi, Dakpa, Mbi; Ngundu (of Bianga/Kouango, Mid-Southern Banda, ISO nue) is not named. The catalog's Ngundu record rests on Cloarec-Heiss 1978 (ngündù de Bianga). Statements taken from Tisserant for ngun1266 should be flagged as Banda-general.
